core: The working definition: communication in healthcare as the exchange of information between patients, families, and the care team (working definition, attributed to the care-team framing shared by AHRQ TeamSTEPPS and MedlinePlus)

Why it matters: communication failures cause harm — AHRQ patient-safety findings that communication failures between providers are a leading cause of preventable error and handoffs are linked to adverse events, with an original example and an honest note that most failures cost rework rather than lives
Verbal vs. nonverbal communication: words, tone, body language, and silence, each named
The four techniques: clear language, active listening, one question at a time, and teach-back, each with one line, plus an original teach-back example
Handoffs: transferring information and responsibility between caregivers, with the SBAR structure (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) attributed to AHRQ/TeamSTEPPS
Barriers: language, hearing, anxiety, and jargon, each named, and the honest framing that communication is the wiring of the whole care system
supporting: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS program page (evidence-based teamwork tools; patients and family caregivers included in healthcare teams; communication as a core module)
AHRQ TeamSTEPPS 3.0 Pocket Guide PDF (SBAR definition; teach-back; handoff; closed-loop communication; brief/clear/specific/timely information competency)

claims.claim: For this lesson, a working definition: communication in healthcare is the exchange of information between patients, families, and the care team; patients and family members are members of the team — MedlinePlus tells patients they can help prevent medical errors by being an active member of their health care team, and AHRQ's TeamSTEPPS program includes patients and family caregivers in the healthcare teams it trains.

Communication failures between providers have been found to be a leading cause of preventable error in studies of closed malpractice claims, and handoffs have been linked to adverse clinical events in settings from the emergency department to the intensive care unit.

A handoff is the process of one healthcare provider updating another on the status of one or more patients for the purpose of handing over responsibility for their care; it can occur at a change of shift, between departments, or when EMS hands a patient to the emergency department.

SBAR is a technique from AHRQ's TeamSTEPPS for communicating critical information that requires immediate attention and action concerning a patient's condition, structured as Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation.

TeamSTEPPS communication competencies include providing brief, clear, specific, and timely information to team members and using closed-loop strategies (call-out, check-back, teach-back) to verify that information was understood.

The teach-back method is a way of checking understanding by asking patients to state in their own words what they need to know or do about their health; the related show-me method confirms patients can perform a specific action.

AHRQ's health-literacy guidance calls for plain, nonmedical language, warns that using jargon and terms patients do not understand is an act of exclusion that can increase healthcare and health disparities, and advises limiting information to one to three need-to-know points.
Effective handoffs require an environment free of interruptions and distractions so the clinician receiving the handoff can listen actively and engage in discussion when necessary.
MedlinePlus advises patients whose provider does not speak their language to call ahead and ask the office to provide an interpreter, and to ask questions until they understand what they are told.
Patients who are more involved with their care tend to get better results, and being an active member of the health care team helps prevent medical errors.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much preventable harm is attributable to communication failure?
positions: AHRQ's PSNet primer reports that communication failures between providers have been found to be a leading cause of preventable error in studies of closed malpractice claims affecting emergency physicians and trainees.
Specific percentages vary by study methodology, setting, and definition of communication failure (malpractice-claims reviews, sentinel-event analyses, and observational studies measure differently).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses AHRQ's qualitative phrasing — 'a leading cause of preventable error' — attributed to the source, and deliberately avoids publishing any specific percentage.

sourceRecords.title: TeamSTEPPS Program (TeamSTEPPS 3.0)
sourceRecords.provider: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200). Supports: TeamSTEPPS is an evidence-based set of teamwork tools aimed at optimizing patient outcomes by improving communication and teamwork skills among healthcare teams, including patients and family caregivers; AHRQ updated TeamSTEPPS in 2023; the TeamSTEPPS 3.0 curriculum includes modules on Communication, Team Leadership, Situation Monitoring, and Mutual Support. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: TeamSTEPPS 3.0 Pocket Guide
sourceRecords.provider: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. PDF read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: SBAR as a technique for communicating critical information that requires immediate attention and action concerning a patient's condition, structured as Situation/Background/Assessment/Recommendation; teach-back as a method to confirm the sender explained clearly and the patient or family member understands by restating in their own words; handoff as a standardized method for transferring information, authority, and responsibility during transitions in care; closed-loop communication via call-outs, check-backs, and teach-backs; the communication competency of providing brief, clear, specific, and timely information. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Handoffs and Signouts (Patient Safety Primer)
sourceRecords.provider: AHRQ Patient Safety Network (PSNet), Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live 2026-08-22 (HTTP 200; primer authored 2019, last reviewed by the UC Davis PSNet editorial team June 2024). Supports: the handoff definition (one provider updating another on the status of one or more patients for the purpose of handing over responsibility for care); handoffs linked to adverse clinical events from the emergency department to the intensive care unit; communication failures between providers as a leading cause of preventable error in studies of closed malpractice claims; the I-PASS standardized handoff bundle and its measured reduction of preventable adverse events; and the requirement of an interruption-free environment with active listening for effective handoffs. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
